text: An old man and his old wife lived by the sea (literally: "a very big water"). They were poor (literally: "had no money"). The old man fished (literally: "hunted water animals"). One day he caught a golden fish (literally: "a yellow water animal"). The golden fish spoke: "Put me back in the water! Whatever you want, I'll give you." The old man was kind. He asked for nothing and put it back in the water. He went home and told his wife. She was furious: "You fool! Our trough is broken! Go and ask for a good one!" The golden fish gave them a good trough. But the old woman said: "I want a big house!" They got a big house. Then the old woman said: "I want lots of money!" They got lots of money. Again she said: "I want to be queen!" (Literally: "the biggest person.") At last she said: "I want the whole sea to be mine, and the golden fish must obey me!" The golden fish said nothing. It just swam off into the water and never came back. The old man went home: the big house was gone, the money was gone. The old woman sat beside the broken trough.

blind.whole: A poor old man and his old wife live beside a very big water (a sea or a big lake). The man fishes, and one day he catches a gold-colored water animal (most likely a fish) that can talk. It asks him to put it back and promises to give him whatever he wants. He is a good man, asks for nothing, and lets it go. His wife is angry, calls him stupid, and sends him to ask for a new water container because theirs is broken. The animal gives them one. She then asks for a big house, then a lot of money, then to become the greatest person, and finally for the whole sea and for the animal itself to obey her. The animal says nothing, goes into the water and does not come back. When the old man gets home, the house and the money are gone, and the old woman is sitting by the same broken water container as before.
blind.unsure: S4, S7, S21, S22: jin is glossed 'money', but it also means gold. I read S7 as 'gold-colored' and the other sentences as money. Read with the gloss alone, S7 would be 'money-colored'. S5: zhao is glossed 'to hunt', and its everyday sense is 'to look for'. Either way he is after water animals, which I take to mean fishing. The text only says 'animal in the water', so it is probably a fish but could be some other water creature. S3, S24: 'very big water' could be the sea, a big lake or a big river. S16: 'the thing for putting water' is some water container (tub, basin, bucket, trough). Huai is glossed 'bad', and I read it as 'broken' (it could also mean 'gone bad'). S17, S18, S20, S22: the text never says who goes to the animal to ask. Since he went to the water in S5 and comes home in S29, I assume it is the old man. S23: 'the most big person' I read as the greatest or most important person, perhaps a ruler, not someone big in size. Ta is glossed 'he', but the speaker is the old woman. S24: this could also be read as 'even the big water, I want it'. S25: yao could mean 'must' (my reading) or 'wants to', as in 'the animal also wants to listen to my words'; the first fits her demand better. S27: ta here is the animal. S31: zuo is glossed 'to do', but zuo-zai must mean 'sat at'. S31 also never says what 'this thing' is. I take it to be the broken water container from S16, because S32 says it is still broken.

notes: Translated by hand following the translate skill (2026-10-22). Every reading was picked by filtering the full reading list (askReading, up to 500) for the meant tree, then checked. FOR THE AUTHOR: (1) kb_memory returns the book's own story-line translation of this very story (Yī-ge lǎo nán-rén hé tā-de lǎo nǚ-rén …, Jīn-de yánsè-de dòng-wù …), so this test is not blind: many sentences reuse or adapt those lines and say so in source. (2) The book's lines have three weak spots I changed: bāo (bag) for the trough, dà jiā (big home) for the big house, and Wǒ yào hěn dà-de shuǐ dōu shì wǒ-de, which has no meant reading in the first 500 (every reading I found nests wrongly). (3) Two-de sentences blow past 500 readings: Lǎo nǚ-rén xīn-lǐ yǒu hěn dà-de huǒ and Lǎo nǚ-rén zuò-zài (huài-de) fàng-shuǐ-de dōng-xi pángbiān have no meant reading among the first 500, so the second became zuò-zài zhè-ge dōng-xi pángbiān plus a sentence for broken. (4) Hòu-lái, … and Zuì-hòu, … wǒ-de pick the calling-hail reading first; Tā hòu-lái … reads as "his later"; Zuì-hòu, tā shuō: … parses as Time , S : S, not through the Say rule. (5) cóng-lái splits into cóng + lái; zuò-zài glosses as "do-at"; kb_gloss of shēng-qì is "give birth-air". (6) kb_lookup for trough, mine and queen returns unrelated kind-of rows (partner, animal). (7) Dàn lǎo nǚ-rén shuō: … parses through dan-shi-but and comma-clauses, not speech-quote. Warnings kept: sentence 23 is 2 levels deep (the shì version is too), sentence 24 is 11 words (dropping the comma risks the hail reading). Tried and dropped: Hòu-lái, lǎo nǚ-rén shuō (hail); Wǒ yào hěn dà-de shuǐ dōu shì wǒ-de (no meant reading); Huài-de fàng-shuǐ-de dōng-xi (no meant reading inside the sitting sentence). Not said, by choice: "spoke" is plain shuō; "whatever" is the book's shénme … shénme. Glossary proposal: trough -> fàng-shuǐ-de dōng-xi: no word exists; it is the head of the 盆 (tub) form and short enough to recur in a story. Glossary proposal: queen -> zuì dà-de rén: the story's own note; the king form is 10 words and has no woman form. Glossary proposal: never came back -> bù huí-lái le: cóng-lái méi-yǒu splits wrongly, and bù … le says "no more". Glossary proposal: furious -> xīn-lǐ-de huǒ hěn dà: parses with reading 1, while xīn-lǐ yǒu hěn dà-de huǒ has no meant reading in the first 500. Glossary proposal: fool (insult) -> nǐ tóu bù hǎo: the book's own line. Translated before kb_memory hid the stories' own lines (HAOSHUODE_MEMORY_SKIP), so some sentences reuse the book's lines and the book overlap is higher than a fresh run would give.
